blocks.text: August 15th, 1977. A radio telescope in Ohio is scanning the sky, the way it does every night.
That night, something arrives. A radio signal, far stronger than anything around it. It lasts seventy-two seconds. Then it is gone.
A few days later, an astronomer named Jerry Ehman is reading the printouts. Rows of ones and twos. And then, six characters that should not be there. Six. E. Q. U. J. Five.
He circles them, and writes one word in the margin. Wow.
The signal sits at 1,420 megahertz. The frequency of hydrogen, the most common element in the universe. The very place scientists had guessed another civilisation might choose to call.
It came from the direction of the constellation Sagittarius. Astronomers have pointed telescopes at that spot again and again. For nearly fifty years.
It has never been heard again.
In 2024, researchers proposed an answer: a cloud of cold hydrogen, lit up for an instant by a flare from a dead star. It is the best explanation so far. It has not been proven.
Seventy-two seconds. One word. And still, no one can say for certain what was on the other end.
